utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good afternoon to you, too. Everyone is here except Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution is as it was yesterday, Mr. McCloskey. The witness is in the courtroom. I take it there are no preliminaries? So perhaps, Mr. McCloskey, you can finish your direct and then we pass on to the cross-examinations. Do we have, more or less, an approximate? You had requested two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that one hour will suffice for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I haven't heard the entire direct, obviously, but I think I predict an hour or 45 minutes. We've changed the order somewhat, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. We will not interfere with that. Mr. Lazarevic, you had indicated an hour and 45 minutes. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We've reorganised ourselves today and I believe we will use 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it, if the others had a conservative time, it's still in that region? Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, 30 minutes, but it could, in fact, be a quarter of an hour or 20 minutes only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa or Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Ten minutes, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think that if your direct -- the rest of your direct is not long, we can finish this witness today. Let's make an effort. I hope he's understood what we are trying to do in order not to keep him here until Wednesday or Thursday. So, Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've reorganised as well, and I hope to be fairly short. But I think we can stay in open session for a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We left off when you were driving an APC and you came to an area of a little school. Can you tell us about that again, just -- I mean, just take up where we left off. As you come into this area there is a school. What happens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I turned the APC around in the direction of the school, in the direction from which I had come. I passed the sports grounds in front of the school and turned around to face the direction I had come from. And the buses and trucks approached the sports grounds and people disembarked and set off in the direction of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, what had Colonel Popovic done when he approached the area of the school in his vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said this yesterday, but upon approaching the school, he turned off in front of a house, maybe a private house, opposite the school. He took a left turn from the road itself, to a house opposite the -- or across the road from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So now you've turned the APC around and you described seeing people get out of the buses, and you described that yesterday. So what else did you see as you were there watching this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what else I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long were you there watching it until you moved on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long it took, but I know that as soon as there was an opening for me to take my APC through, I took it through and drove back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. In the past we have an estimate of roughly how many buses and trucks you saw there. Do you remember how many buses and trucks you saw before you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe ten vehicles were emptied before I departed, but I cannot remember how many vehicles stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If roughly ten vehicles emptied before you departed, were there still vehicles on the road as you left the area of the school, going back towards Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other vehicles. They did not empty all the vehicles before I departed. There were vehicles with people still on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Aside from the ten that emptied, roughly, how many vehicles, just roughly, do you think you drove by that still had people on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many more vehicles there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: More than five?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot recall. If I knew it was more than five, I would have told you; if I knew it was less than five, I would have told you, but I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Those old buses - you were a bus driver - can you estimate how many people fit on those kinds of buses that you saw used when they were all filled up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that there were no people standing on the buses, in the aisle, so they were not overcrowded. A single bus may take between 40 and 50 passengers on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And before you left, did you speak to Colonel Popovic at all, or did he speak to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw that there was an opening for me so that I could drive my APC through, I set off. And upon passing by Colonel Popovic, he stopped me and told me that I should stay there, but I told him that I could not stay because I was ordered by Major Nikolic to return, because of some other obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that true? Had Momir Nikolic ordered you to return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't order me -- for me to return to attend to some other duties. I did not feel like staying there any longer. There was no reason for me there. If people were taken there to be exchanged or if they were waiting for the right time to be exchanged, then there was no reason for me to stay there. So this is why I turned back and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a photo. It's marked PO1691. It should come up on your screen. Do you recognise that? Let's make sure it's there. Do you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is supposed to be the school where people were disembarked when they came there. I turned around next to this fence, from the spot where this photo was taken, and the vehicles pulled up beside the sports grounds. They disembarked passengers across that sports ground. And by the wall of the school, there was a fence, one and a half metres from the wall of the school, and they passed between the fence and the wall of the school, moving towards the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does this look like the school where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And what do you do when you leave the area of the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove back to my headquarters, the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade, and came back to my military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to go over an exhibit with you. I know you've seen it before. It's called the -- well, the military police, the log of the military police, something to that effect. Can you tell us what that is and we'll -- you'll be able to see different entries from it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it may be easier if I just give him the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. Just hand it over to him. If he's seen it already, as far as you state, then you just put the questions you wish. Do we have them also in e-court, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that should be coming up pretty soon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the 65 ter number is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 220. Sorry. And if we could -- that's 30 June, if we could just start with 11 July, that would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While they are getting to 11 July, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe go into private session, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can start the first cross-examination now or we can have the break now, but I see that Mr. Krgovic is already on his feet. Mr. Krgovic is appearing for General Gvero in this case and he will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a couple of questions in connection with an event that you described to the Prosecutor and which you described in your statement in November in 2002, I think. You mentioned on that occasion the members of the DutchBat who were billeted in Bratunac, and in an interview with the Prosecutor, you said that these members of the DutchBat fled to the Serbian side because they were afraid of Muslim attacks, because the Muslims wanted to take their weapons away and they wanted to murder them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Among those were people from the OP Mike; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the titles of their observation posts. I believe they were at Jaglici. They had a check-point there, at Jaglici. There were some other elevations, et cetera, but they had observation posts around Srebrenica and they had their own official titles. The DutchBat had their own official titles or names for these. I remember this name Jaglici. I remember well that they said they had come from the Jaglici observation post but I never knew where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the Dutch soldiers fled from the Jaglici OP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and from other points. Some came from Jaglici; others from another. I stated here, if you remember, when I discussed the stay at Konjevic Polje, that two members of the DutchBat came without any vehicles, carrying just their personal sidearms and a knapsack, rifle and a knapsack, came to the Konjevic Polje intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you performed the security services during their stay at the high school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did so for a very long time. We would take them to breakfast, lunch and dinner, to the kitchen of the Bratunac Brigade HQ. For instance, one military policeman would escort them so that nobody from among the soldiers or citizens would harm them in any way. That military person would take them and escort them to the kitchen and then back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor, while interviewing you, asked you whether you knew why they were not later returned to Potocari base, and you said that they didn't want to go back because they didn't know what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. They didn't want to do because they were safer here. Maybe they were afraid that they would be engaged by their own battalion in an action, an operation, and they simply abandoned their HQ at Potocari, which was the main base of UNPROFOR in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will broach another subject. Answering the Prosecutor's question on whether anything of importance was going on in July, immediately before the fall of Srebrenica, you responded that there was a period where there were daily incidents and attacks of Muslim forces from Srebrenica against the villages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have an objection. At this point, I don't see how this is relevant. And time is of the essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since the thesis of the Defence is that the attack against the enclave was carried out because of military reasons, because, in the period immediately before the attack, Muslims had carried out frequent attacks and terrorist acts and attacked, that this was the trigger to the attack against the enclave. And the thesis of the Defence is that the attack against the enclave was a pure military target and goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I can be of some help. For many years now, we have agreed with the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely what my colleagues and I are trying to -- because I am under the impression that this is, in a way, dealt with already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can briefly state the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The position is that Muslims did attack outside the enclave and that this did provide military justification for the Serb troops to attack Srebrenica. However, it has been our position that the attack on Srebrenica had a dual motive: One was military and it had some legitimacy; two was to take out the Muslim population from the enclave, which is a crime against humanity. And that when there are two motives, one legitimate and one illegitimate, our charges are based on the illegitimate one. We have never suggested - and you won't see it in Mr. Butler's report - that Naser Oric and his units did not attack. In fact, we have provided the documents that showed that it was policy to attack and tie down the Muslim forces to be -- or tie down the Serb forces to prevent them from going to the Sarajevo front where the real battles in 1995 were going on. This is all part of our case, for this continuing area. And now I'm taking up too much time, so I will be quiet. But this is the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Krgovic and the rest of you, I would look at the indictment, see what the charges are, concentrate on those charges and the alleged responsibility of your clients, and forget history. You're not going to rewrite history, Mr. Krgovic, neither you, nor anybody else, for that matter. And I think what is being conceded by Mr. McCloskey goes even beyond what has been decided in some cases here. So I suggest you go straight to what is relevant. I mean, you're not defending here the entire VRS or the Main Staff or Republika Srpska or the Serb -- I mean, it's only your clients that are indicted in this case. It's neither Serbia, nor the Serbian people, nor the VRS. It's your clients that are being indicted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a real waste of time that we have to have our attention address these matters when -- they are relevant, I mean, there is no question that they are not relevant. But you should be concentrating on what is really more important in this case, and that's the alleged responsibility of your clients, and, of course, whether the events actually took place or not, because that's another fundamental part of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, but there is another thing here. My client, among other things, has been charged with providing false information and that, in his statements for the press, misrepresented certain facts; specifically, one document cited by the Prosecutor in his introduction, referring to my client's statement about Srebrenica, has been construed by the Prosecutor in one way, but the Defence of General Gvero is that the facts that he enumerated in his public statements really did occur in the way that he described them. This is why I want to check some facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is not being charged for having given false information. He's being charged with what he's being charged with in this indictment. That's why my invitation was to you to concentrate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I say something, Your Honour? I accept the Court's invitation, and I tried to shorten it yesterday with a motion. But if we are going to address only the charges in the indictment, then I think I need to restate my motion and reiterate it again, because those aren't the charges, as we discussed yesterday, on the issue of reburial. And I agree with the Court's logic. With all due respect, however, I don't think that we applied that logic with respect to this motion, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, your client is not charged with reburial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to hear you say. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is nothing in the indictment that says that your client is charged with reburial. This is what I'm trying to make you understand. And I wouldn't like to waste more time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which pertains to my client, which says [In English] the statement concerning the attacks on the enclave in order to assist in the take-down of the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. McCloskey is telling you precisely that did happen - this is what he's saying - but other things happened, too, and the attack on Srebrenica was a double-pronged operation. One was meant to reach one target and the other was meant to obtain another -- Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To try to save time, I would like to meet with counsel. We can go over the statements that his client made. I will agree with him that they are not all false, and I can show him which ones I don't believe are false. Some of them, in the exact area he's talking about, are not false, though false statements is a part of the indictment. But I'm sure we can agree on which ones aren't false, and the ones related to Muslim attacks may very well not be false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I think it's time to have the break now. We'll have a 25-minute break. In the meantime, see if you can discuss further with Mr. McCloskey on this, and then you proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so let it be known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break of 25 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic is going first. I leave it in your wisdom and discretion to tell us when we need to go into private session, all right? So you know how we've been going the past two days, and there are some issues we are dealing with in private session, some issues in open.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be mindful of that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Zivanovic is appearing for Colonel Popovic and he will be cross-examining you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will not be addressing you by your name because you have protective measures. I would want to direct your attention to the day when you escorted, in the APC, some vehicles holding refugees in -- all the way to a school near Zvornik. If I remember correctly, you said that you saw Lieutenant Colonel Popovic park his car to -- rather, on the left-hand side of the school, opposite the location where the school is; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You went straight on and entered the yard of the school compound, or rather, the sports grounds, or did you make a U-turn before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I passed by the school grounds, and made a U-turn to that spot that we were able to see on the photograph. I'm not sure whether this is the spot where the roads fork off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If I understand you correctly, you didn't stay there for too long. You weren't able to tell us how long, in fact, it took you to head back.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long it was, but it wasn't that long after several vehicles were emptied and the people went to the school, at which point I had an opening in the road and was able to head back, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as you proceeded, as you had the opening in the road, you were able to leave the area smoothly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before leaving, you saw Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, who asked you to stay there for sometime still.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you stated, but let me ask you this: Did he stay on the spot where he stood at the time, next to the parked vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was next to the parked vehicles throughout that time and stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I already sense that we are going too fast, all right? I didn't tell the witness this before, neither did you. You're both speaking the same language; therefore, there is no need for interpretation between you. But whatever is being said by you is being interpreted to us. So if you don't allow a short pause between question and answer, the interpreters can't translate what you're saying in its entirety. So please allow a short pause between question and answer, all right? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We received a piece of information here about the interview you had with the Prosecution before this trial commenced, and there, I was able to read that Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, as he stood by his car, when you saw him, that he spoke to some persons in civilian clothes. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were some people there in civilian clothes. There were even women and children there, whether they had their homes nearby. But all around the school there were people observing. Whether he communicated with anyone or not, I don't know. At any rate, there were people in his immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you told us that the military police had, among other things, the task of protecting prisoners from the angered residents of Bratunac who had lost their relatives, family members, friends and so on. You also said that the police took care of this along the road on which the prisoners were being transported. Did you have occasion to see something of the sort on that particular location near Zvornik where you came with the vehicles, since you say you saw a lot of civilians there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a few civilians there; however, there was no reaction on their part whatsoever, either good or bad. They simply stayed aside and looked on as we arrived with the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the civilians, the same ones who were there where Lieutenant Colonel Popovic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I read your earlier statements and had occasion to read your earlier evidence before this Tribunal. I was under the impression that your general recollection of the events in Srebrenica became quite poor in time. I wanted to ask you this -- now, I could exhaustively present to you your evidence; however, I would like to ask you this: The discrepancies or differences in your testimony, can they be ascribed to your poor memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they can be ascribed to my poor recollection of these events, because I do not talk about these events to anyone in order to refresh my memory repeatedly. However, what remained etched in my memory, as much as I do remember, I do convey to you the way I remember them. For instance, five years ago, my memory must have been much better because the lapse of time was shorter, six or five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that at the time you gave some statements, which was six or eight years after the events of Srebrenica, that even at that time your memory faded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I didn't have anything to make me remember these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Today, and previously, you were asked to talk about the events that took place only in two consecutive days, or perhaps even three consecutive days. I also noticed in your earlier statements, where you emphasised this, that these events tended to become confused in your memory, to get all mixed up. Would you stand by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it, therefore, be correct if I said that you're talking about matters that you remember, but that you cannot fully guarantee that the way you remember these matters is accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall all the details, and I find it quite logical. I can't remember, and I don't know of anyone else who could recall when he had seen a person, whether it was in the morning, in the afternoon, or what they were specifically doing. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your return from that location near Zvornik, you saw Mr. Momir Nikolic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you told him where you had been and what you'd been doing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell him that you were given the task of safely escorting the convoy holding prisoners to a location near Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that I was tasked with staying near the vehicle, and that I didn't know where I was going. I told him that, as I was following the vehicle in front of me, holding Colonel or Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, that I thus reached a village beyond Zvornik, that I pulled up there and I told him the way things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell him that you followed the convoy but without Lieutenant Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic was not in my vehicle. He was in the vehicle in front of me. I didn't know where we were heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood what you were saying. However, my question is: Did you tell Mr. Momir Nikolic that you led the convoy without mentioning Lieutenant Popovic as being in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I told him, but if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you tell him that, among other things, your task was to escort the convoy and that you should return as soon as the prisoners were safely put up on that location near Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell him that my task was -- or this was my knowledge: The prisoners were supposed to go there in order to be exchanged all for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've said that. But my question is: Did you tell this to Momir Nikolic? Did you tell him what I've just asked you? Did you tell him about what happened? You don't need to go into these other matters. You've already mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that I did not wait for the entire convoy to disembark, and that as soon as I was able to pass along the road, I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And did you tell him that the transport was secured by the military policemen from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that convoy, there were no members of the Bratunac Brigade military police. I didn't send them, nor could I have sent them. I didn't know whether there were any or if there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell Momir Nikolic at the time anything concerning Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, except for saying that you received the instructions from him to escort the prisoners to that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that he had asked that I stay at the point when I wanted to return, and that I had told him that I was unable to stay behind because I had obligations to attend to, obligations that were given to me by Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this was the only thing you told him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've heard this, but before this Tribunal and before the Bosnian judiciary, you hold the status of a suspect. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this is the case, indeed, well, what can I do about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the other two persons you mentioned here also hold the same status, who were with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know. Are you aware that the other two persons were heard in a proceedings before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I told you use your --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I avoided mentioning any names to avoid them being connected with the witness, and this is why I wanted us to remain in open session. But now that this matter has been resolved, my intention was to elicit from the witness information whether he knew that these two witnesses appeared in trials connected with this case at this Tribunal, and this was the sole intention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I need to answer, my answer would be this: I don't know about Petrovic, but I do know about this Popovic, that he was involved in the process against Naser Oric, in the trial. I saw it on television. And that information was such that there was an incident in the courtroom at that point, and this is how I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, the witness has just testified in open session about these two other witnesses, but to which extent this could be connected back to his identity, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question would be, it seems to me that you've already been summoned by Bosnian authorities to give statement, as well as the other two individuals who were there with you. Is it known to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with them being summoned. I know that I've been summoned. Maybe it was the Srebrenica commission or whatnot. Is that what you mean? Maybe these are police inquiries to determine the facts of the Srebrenica case. Anyway, I don't know. I can't be specific, but I was summoned to the police station on several occasions and criminal -- forensics personnel from Bijeljina came and they interviewed me about this, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you have occasion to talk about those summons with those two individuals, and did you discuss with them matters that you're going to be interviewed about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss with them the subject matter of this examination. Everybody can testify to what they remember. I cannot restore anybody else's memory, and I don't want anybody else to restore my memory. I don't want to be prepared or primed because, frankly speaking, I get confused. If I remember something, I remember it, and there is a reason why I remember something. But if there are immaterial things that I don't see as important, like when I saw somebody, et cetera, that I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note there was overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are overlapping again. Could you kindly repeat your question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What priming do you mean that may result in you being confused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the proofing by the Prosecution and citing my earlier statements, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Zivanovic. I understand that the Beara Defence team will be cross-examining you now, and that's Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- who is lead counsel defending Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Upon consultation with Mr. Beara, we will not have any questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Ostojic. That takes us to Mr. Stojanovic, who is defending, together with Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Borovcanin in this case. He will be cross-examining you now. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, Witness. I would like to ask to go into private session just for the first question, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Indeed, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a problem with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Immediate superior, the witness said, immediate superior. The question was: You received orders from Momir Nikolic. Answer: My immediate superior was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we had problems with the interpretation because we heard French in our headsets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you received the information from Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was my immediate superior. He was the chief of security at Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I don't want any confusion. If you read line 13 of this page, the interpreter said the question -- he is supposedly repeating your question, Mr. Stojanovic. "The question was: You received orders from Momir Nikolic." And then in line 19, again, it's you now, Mr. Stojanovic: "So you received the information from Momir Nikolic." Perhaps you wish to address the question of whether it's orders that we are talking about or mere information, because during that short interval, when we were not receiving interpretation, something might have been said which would need to go in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the question was: You received orders from Momir Nikolic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next, I'd like to ask you, Mr. Witness, this: Did you have occasion, during your holding the post of the commander of military police platoon, to learn that Momir Nikolic issued direct orders on the use of members of military police without consulting you or without you knowing about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would happen very frequently. I could not constantly be there where I was supposed to be at the seat of the military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, some members of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade was located at Potocari, under direct orders of Momir Nikolic. Do you personally know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even when I was at the location where the military police was deployed, Momir Nikolic would come and issue direct orders to some individuals about what they were supposed to do. For instance, "You go there," "You go somewhere else," or "You, five of you, come with me." Then, of course, they had to observe such an order. He did not address me by saying, "You give me an X number of policemen. I'm taking them to do that." He had no duty to address me in this way or to inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask you to go back into private session, Your Honours, for a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go back to open session, please -- private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Stojanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether Bratunac Brigade military police members were at Potocari on the night between 12th and 13th of July, the ones that you enumerated just a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were not there, because, in my opinion, General Mladic was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would ask you to look jointly at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask you to help me with the e-court. Exhibit 4D16, Your Honours, this is another -- I'm retrieving a statement containing the guilty plea of Momir Nikolic, and I'd like us to focus on the last sentence on page 2 and the first two rows on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have it on the screen first, because otherwise we will not be able to follow you. Okay. It seems to -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility, it reads: "In joint action with these units, I coordinated and supervised the transport of women and children for Kladanj, and the separation and apprehension of able-bodied Muslim men." My question would be: From discussions with Momir Nikolic, are you aware of this activity and these tasks of his?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last time I testified before this Tribunal, I gave a statement in connection with -- and, as far as I knew, that was an agreement between Nikolic and the OTP. And that agreement stated, it seems to me, that Nikolic accepted guilt and that he stated that he was in charge of everything, that he was superior than the Main Staff of the VRS and the Commander-in-Chief, General Ratko Mladic. I gave to the OTP, and the OTP had it translated into English and this document was given back to me, but I did not take it with me this time. In that document, it is stated that Momir Nikolic had planned the action to take Srebrenica, that he commanded the action to take Srebrenica, that he had carried out the separation of able-bodied men from women and children, that he was in charge of transporting them, that he committed murders, ordered murders, redeployment of mass graves. And I stated that this was not so because nobody could have done anything without Mladic. Mladic was the commander, and Nikolic could not have planned and carried out all these. I know that he couldn't do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you leave a possibility that he was carrying out such orders; yes or no? Do you know or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say this: I think that he did not carry out these orders. Had he done so, then a military police or some unit subordinated to him would have been involved in that. If he did it on his own, then this is quite another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you about the 13th of July. Together with Momir Nikolic, you took the UN APC to drive to Konjevic Polje; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a light blue Golf with rotating lights and a megaphone mounted on top of it; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That Golf joined you at Konjevic Polje, when you arrived there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Golf did not join us. I never saw where it came from. But he wasn't -- it wasn't there when we reached the intersection. But after a while - I have to slow down because of the interpreters - after a while, after we reached Konjevic Polje, Momir Nikolic told us that we had to follow this vehicle which was 200 or 300 metres away from the intersection in the area. I could see it because visibility was fine. It was standing by the road. And when that vehicle started, I started to follow it, and I kept the same distance between the APC and that vehicle at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember and do you know who drove the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many persons there were in the vehicle or who drove the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But judging by its colour, the vehicle belonged to the civilian police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Today, the Prosecutor asked you about the position of Ljubomir Borovcanin, and you said that he had left the area before these events concerning Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how long before that, a year. But at any rate, he left Bratunac and wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But we agreed that in July of 1995 he was not a member of the civilian police, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the position he held at the time, he had nothing to do with the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which position he held, but he didn't have any dealings with the police that was there, since he had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Together with that vehicle, the -- rather, apart from that vehicle and your APC, there was another UN APC there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was driven by the members of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether they were members of the Bratunac Brigade. As they arrived in Konjevic Polje, they set off for Milici. I don't know how far up they went. At any rate, we stopped at the point where I told you and they went straight on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if at the time the Bratunac Brigade had a megaphone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade did not have a megaphone. That vehicle had a loud-speaker mounted on the vehicle next to the rotating light, or rather, two rotating lights, and in between they had a loud-speaker mounted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see now on e-court Exhibit 65 ter P220. That's the military police log. I want to direct your attention to the pages which hold entries for 23 and 24 July 1995. Could we have the page in the English version for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. In the meantime ... Your Honour, it is quite possible that the section I'm referring to hasn't been translated as yet. This is the document given to us by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid the last entry's date is the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. By your leave, I would read out one relevant passage. It's only one sentence, and then this would enable us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to one portion of the text, Witness. It says, if you can follow: "Because of the numerous cases of apprehension or bringing in, we had to inform them over the megaphone." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what this is about, and what is this megaphone about, contained in this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The megaphone must have been borrowed from the brigade headquarters. It's the normal bull horn, hand-held. It wasn't the one that would be mounted on a vehicle. Battery-operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would again ask us to see on e-court 4D16, and to turn to page 5, to the second paragraph in the English version. In the B/C/S version, that would be page 5, third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd ask you again to look at a portion of Momir Nikolic's guilty plea statement, where he says, when describing this day, that Mile Petrovic was seated on the APC and, over the megaphone, called upon Muslim men to surrender. Is it possible that this was the way it actually happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't happen that way. We didn't have any megaphone with us. Nikolic even stated in one of his statements that Mile Petrovic drove that APC. I cannot say that Mile Petrovic drove the APC when I drove it. Now, whether this is the way he remembers these events, or maybe he has other reasons for saying this, but I want to recount the events as they happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Still, would you allow the possibility that you didn't know of the existence -- of the possible existence of a megaphone in the other APC? You didn't see anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see anything of the sort, and, besides, it wasn't that APC that followed the vehicle, it was my APC that followed the vehicle. And I wasn't able to hear what was said because of the noise produced by the APC engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session again for the next two questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help us and tell us anything about the burial of the dead at the UN base between the 12th and the 13th, within the UN base compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that there were any dead people in the UN base at all. I know that the sick and wounded were transferred to the infirmary of the health centre in Bratunac that was secured by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Bratunac Brigade military police at one point take control of the UN base facility itself after they left Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the UN, the DutchBat, left the base, the military police secured the facility itself and the property that had been left behind. Some 20 containers may have been left behind, of some sort of equipment, and this was secured by the military police until further notice, or I don't know what happened to it, what became of it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Part of their military equipment was left behind at the base, and you secured it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until what time did you provide security of the equipment and who did you hand the facility and the equipment to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the equipment was handed over to. I know that the military police secured the facility for quite a long time, the perimeter, the compound of the base itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the equipment safe thereby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm nearing the end of my examination. In view of what you did, both in your civilian career and in wartime, I meant in civilian police and military police, did you have occasion to see the possibility of regular police being subordinated to the army in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who commanded whom and who issued orders to whom. I don't even know who issued orders to me any longer. As I said, it is quite possible that an element of a unit or a unit itself is given over to a commander's competence. For instance, the entire military police platoon or an element, a part of the military police platoon, or any other unit, may have been given to the jurisdiction of a different unit for a specific task. And for as long as the command to which the unit was subordinated does not indicate to the unit that it can go back to its initial chain of command, they stay within or under the formation to which they were temporarily assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at any time during the war in a position to see that the army was subordinated to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a thing never happened, that the army would be subordinated to the civilian police. The army was more numerous. There was a war on and there was no way in which the army could have been subordinated to the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me finish with this question: You've heard of Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've heard that for a while he was the commander of the police station at Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't sure whether he was the commander or the deputy commander or assistant commander. I know that he was in the Bratunac police station, holding a certain position. He wasn't a regular policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This wasn't, or rather, this was after the period during which you were the policeman at the police station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a policeman there in early 1992 for some two or three months, and Mr. Borovcanin wasn't in the area of Bratunac municipality at the time at all. It was, perhaps, a year or two years or three years later that he came to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, in the community where you live in Bratunac and the surrounding area, anything bad about the person called Ljubomir Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him that well, but pretty well. I know that he was never a bad man toward anyone. This was a quite a small town, and any news, be it good or bad, is spread around quickly. I know that he was a good man, and what else can I tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. If I could only ask you to move into private session for just a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let's move to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Madam Nikolic is defending Mr. Nikolic in this case, not the Momir Nikolic that you knew but someone else. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd like to bring you back to your journey to Zvornik, to the moment when you departed Bratunac with the convoy. Yesterday, you testified that this happened two hours before mid-day, so that would be around 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I put it this way. I said that I was positioned there at a certain spot, and that after that, I was moved twice to the departure point.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, on the two occasions when you were moved, that took a long time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You waited for the convoy to be formed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably it was very slow in forming, but while I took the fuel at the turning-off point to the brigade headquarters, whether the convoy had been forming at that time, but when I turned around and saw this convoy, as far as I could see, I cannot tell you whether some other vehicles joined the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My question pertained to a long period of time necessary for establishing this convoy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After those two repositionings, did you depart for Zvornik, around 2.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, really, what the hour was when we departed, but I was there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Even approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even approximately. It was a summer day. I know it was a very hot day. I couldn't have gauged the exact hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could I refresh your memory by quoting your testimony in the Blagojevic case. Page 3678 of the transcript in the Blagojevic case, during cross-examination by my colleague, he put to you a similar question and you answered that you waited quite a long time, and at one point you said: "[In English] I don't know how long. Perhaps about one hour, one hour 30, until 2.00, we left from that place."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as I said now, I do not recall when we departed. Maybe 1.30, maybe 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The journey to Zvornik and that school took you one hour, approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which speed we drove at. The instruments showed miles in that APC, so I can't be specific about the speed. We couldn't move fast because the column was long and Colonel Popovic set the pace. I couldn't overtake him. I couldn't be faster than his vehicle. And probably Colonel Popovic was checking in the wing mirror whether the column was following him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can we say one --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, one and a half hours. Well, the distance between Bratunac and Zvornik is 44 kilometres, and then 6, 7 additional kilometres, maybe 50 kilometres to reach that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you reached the school around 3.00, half past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you reached that point, you said that you did not leave the APC; you stayed on it. You mentioned what was the situation, that there were civilians around. Did you notice any prisoners within the school building when you reached that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if there were some prisoners in the school, I could not have seen them. I don't recall whether there were any windows in the gym, and if there are any windows on the gym, they would be positioned very high up. So I did not notice any people within the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you returned to Bratunac in the following days, did you report to Mr. Momir Nikolic that on the 14th of July, many Muslim prisoners were detained in schools and buildings in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that school but I did not see any other schools. I didn't know how this -- what was the name of that place to explain where we were. I just said where we were and that the people stayed there probably to be exchanged all at once, or maybe in groups, and transported to the territory of Sapna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 4D16 put up (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, Madam Nikolic, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The interpreters are hearing some strange noise and the French channel from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it. I am informed by the interpreter who is on line at the moment that he, at least, is hearing strange noises and also interpretation in French or conversation in French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It stopped just now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now it seems to be all right. I just want to make sure that we can proceed in perfect shape. Yes, Ms. Nikolic, sorry for the interruption. Please go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will put just one more question to you. The same document, page 4, paragraph 9. I'm going to ask you a question and you may take a look at the text, if you and I should disagree about this. When you were at Konjevic Polje, you stayed there at the intersection for a long time on your APC. Do you recall the passage of General Mladic, who stopped there and received a report from Momir Nikolic and who stayed for a while in conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what he stated. But I'm trying to sort out this memory for myself. I think that General Mladic passed that point in a Puch vehicle and that he was escorted, maybe a military police escort, from the Bratunac Brigade military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he stop and did Momir Nikolic report to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him stopping or receiving a report. At any rate, he did not stay there long. Maybe they conversed, but I don't remember any formal report being given and any longer conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, Madam Fauveau, who is defending General Miletic, will start her cross-examination. Thank you. We will have a break at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honour, that I will be able to finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, on page 76 of the transcript, you said that the Muslims had been detained for one night after the enclave fell in a school in Bratunac. I just wanted to clarify one point. You, yourself, were not in these schools or around these schools where the Muslims were being held.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in the vicinity of the school, nor in the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the unit of the military police of Bratunac were in charge of securing the Hotel Fontana, together with civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but I have to make a remark on when this happened. Civilian police did not secure the Fontana Hotel on a permanent basis, throughout this process. They would secure -- the civilian police would secure the hotel together with the military police only when meetings were being held. I know of a meeting with the representatives of the Muslim population, of UNPROFOR, and most probably representatives of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you were not standing before the schools in Bratunac when the Muslim prisoners were detained there. How do you know which unit was actually there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I knew this or that unit, and I said that I didn't know whether this unit came from Bratunac brigade at all -- at all. So I didn't say that I knew which unit it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But how, in that case, can you tell that it was a military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How could I know? Maybe somebody told me which unit it was, but I don't know who was there then. I know there weren't civilian police there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said - this was on page 35 of yesterday's transcript - that when some people belonging to the Main Staff and the Drina Corps arrived in Bratunac, the command post of the Drina Corps was located in the Hotel Fontana. I would like to ask you this question: Do you know what a command post of the Drina Corps would be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Drina Corps was Krstic. I can't remember his given name. General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You haven't really answered my question, but I shall rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, what happened to Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He's left for the day, Your Honour. Could I apologise to the Bench? I, perhaps, should have mentioned it. I thought it prudent that rather than highlight it, he just be allowed to leave. But if it was remiss of me not to mention it, I apologise, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It should be the practice that we should be informed, but it's all right. Thank you for letting us know. Is Mr. Sarapa going to cross-examine this witness or the Pandurevic Defence team, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believe that we are going to be through by the time for the break. I have one question, one topic to cover, and I believe I'll be finished quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will be talking about 1992, the beginning of the war, before the attack on the army. You said that there were families leaving Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: These were Serbian families, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Serbian families, and that was the way I left Tuzla. I just couldn't leave, walk out on my job, so I asked to be placed on annual leave in order to find a safe shelter for my family, so I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you please specify what were the circumstances which dictated your departure from there? Can you specify the reasons which prompted you to leave Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, on several occasions, the word was that the Green Berets had made an incursion into the town, that they had taken control of the MUP and other institutions, and this instilled unrest among the Serb population and the other population as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Would you say that you felt insecure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no questions from the Bench, which means that your testimony ends here, sir. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence in this case. Our staff will assist you, to facilitate your return back home. On behalf of everyone present here, we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just making sure that the curtains are put down before he leaves the courtroom. So now the position is, we agreed yesterday that, in anticipation that this witness won't finish today, the other one won't be brought over. In any case, we are adjourned until Wednesday of this coming week -- next week. There has been a further filing from the Prosecution requesting protective measures for PW-98. I have cancelled it from my -- if someone can assist me with the number. There is a fresh motion anyway for protective measures for this new witness. Do I take it that we can proceed along the previous lines? Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much. And tomorrow is the deadline for the filing on the proofing chart. We extended the time limit until the 10th. Will that keep you awake all night, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I think because of those extensions, that we are all relatively sane and you should get something. I'm sure it won't be perfect, but a lot of hard work has gone into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is Your Honour going to deal with the exhibits for the last witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you. Witness 98, yes, not PW-98. I apologise to you. Yes, exhibits, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The pseudonym sheet, P02290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That will remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the 65 ter 220, which is that Bratunac Brigade military daily order book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In its entirety or just the page that -- I think we can proceed with it in its entirety. It would spare us having to go through it in bits and pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And if there are any other pages that someone wants translated, we can always request that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from any of the Defence teams? I see none or I hear none. They are both so admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noticed it's 236 pages in B/C/S. Do we need them all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. What I would suggest is this: That if the Defence want the translation of the entire document, it will, of course, be done. If you're content with having specific parts of the document translated into English, then we'll do that. I mean, it's -- Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My only suggestion - this doesn't, of course, really involve my client - is that my learned friend now specify on the record which pages in the original he wants admitted as an exhibit so there is no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I think, if I understood well, even upon my own invitation, it's the entire document that is being introduced in its original language, that is B/C/S. Now, out of that document, only 21 pages have been, so far, translated into English, and that's because, for the purposes of -- for the Prosecutor's own convenience and utility, I mean, he only needed those 21 pages. Usually, the practice we have adopted here is that if there is a demand from any of the Defence teams to have further pages from that document translated into English, we'll undertake to do that. If not, the situation remains as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, my confusion was that wasn't, basically, the practice in my previous case. Thank you for explaining that. Needless to say, for this exhibit, I've got no objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I was not aware that we were talking about 237 pages. We just usually look at July. But it's probably easier to go with the 237, from our perspective, but that is a lot of extra pages that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But we are talking of a right here, and we'll protect that right, if we come to that or we need to come to that. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The English translation, I believe, is from 30 June to about 20 July, and those are the main focus of the Prosecution's case, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the rest can become relevant particularly in relation to names, components of the units, and so on and so forth. But I wouldn't involve myself in that. If there is a specific request from any of the Defence teams, we will deal with it as it arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One of the Defence referred to an entry from the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any of the Defence team wishes to tender any documents? All right. Mr. Zivanovic? Madam Fauveau? No. I think we can safely adjourn, and I wish you a safe -- a happy weekend. Mr. McCloskey wants to stay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't really, but I do, again, bring up my offer that I'm willing to talk for two minutes about what I think of that witness and what to look for in other evidence and what other evidence to connect with him. I welcome to hear counsel's two minutes on the witness as well, for whatever that's worth. But, again, it's just an offer. It may or may not be of help to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you take a position on this, what Mr. McCloskey said, that he is offering to address us for about two minutes on what he thinks about this witness and what to look for in other evidence and what other evidence to connect him? Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We haven't consulted with all the parties of the Defence, Your Honour. But, yes, we do take a position. If we want to have a closing argument, we may; if we want to discuss every witness, we should at the end of his testimony. That would be fair. Why this one? I do have particular comments which, if the Court allows, I'd like to address about this witness. I don't know that it would be the proper route to take. And I understand the problems that -- or I think I understand the problems my learned friend has with the witness, but I don't think it's appropriate, quite candidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I think we will classify this as pleasures yet to come. With that, we'll adjourn. I thank everyone for having overstayed with us for these extra five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.50 p.m.,
